title: Latency Budgets and Where Time Goes
objectives: Decompose tick-to-trade latency into named stages and assign per-stage budgets
Estimate orders of magnitude for propagation, switching, kernel and processing costs (clearly approximate)
Distinguish fixed physical costs from costs software can influence
Use a latency budget to accept or reject a design
motivation: 'Make it fast' is not an engineering goal. A trading system that must react within a few microseconds needs an explicit ledger: how many nanoseconds for the network, the kernel, the parse, the decision, the risk check, the send? This lesson builds that ledger, the latency budget, because every later optimisation is a claim against it.

blocks.md: **Tick-to-trade** latency is the time from a market-data packet *arriving at your NIC* to your order packet *leaving it*, decision time included. Nothing else counts: backtests, research and dashboards live outside the budget. The path decomposes into stages, each with an owner and a cost. The numbers below are **orders of magnitude, not guarantees**, real values depend on NICs, kernel, CPU and venue, but the discipline is the point: measure each stage, write its cost in the budget, and defend every microsecond against the total.

rows: Physics: light in glass ≈ 2x10^8 m/s. Not optimisable in code
Fewer hops is a design choice

blocks.md: Treat the budget as a **contract**, not a wish list: the sum of stage allowances plus margin must not exceed the target, and every new feature must buy its microseconds from another stage. Note also what the budget *excludes*: the venue's matching time and the trip across town are real delays, but they belong to the end-to-end round trip, not to tick-to-trade, conflating the two is how teams chase numbers no local optimisation can reach. Your budget covers exactly what you own: the NIC-to-NIC span of your own machines.

A latency budget is an accounting document: the target tick-to-trade time, decomposed into every component that spends time, each with an owner and a measured cost. Its discipline is the same as any budget, components must *sum* to the total, every number must be *measured* not guessed, and any overrun must be *paid for* somewhere. Teams that skip the budget discover latency the way individuals discover debt: all at once, in a crisis.

blocks.title: A realistic budget, wire-to-wire (illustrative, exchange colo)
items: **Wire + switch hop**: 800 ns. Photon in fibre plus one switch, this is physics; you cannot optimise it, only shorten the path.
**NIC + driver**: 2,500 ns. Interrupt coalescing is a *choice* here: batching raises throughput and p50 but wrecks p99, a budget line, not a free lunch.

**Kernel network stack**: 3,200 ns in a standard stack. This is the line that kernel-bypass (DPDK, Solarflare/OpenOnload, AF_XDP) exists to delete, but each bypass moves work into your process and your responsibility.

**Decode + strategy + risk checks + order build**: 8,000 ns. The only line that is *yours* end-to-end: the strategy logic, pre-trade risk (position limits, rate limits, self-trade checks) and FIX/OUCH serialisation.

**Total**: ~14.5 µs tick-to-trade. Comfortably fast for most strategies; HFT market makers target single-digit microseconds and pay for it in every line above. The budget makes the *next* decision obvious: the strategy block is 55% of the total, so micro-optimising the kernel stack first would be misallocation.

blocks.title: Averages lie about the tail
blocks.md: A budget satisfied at the mean and blown at p99 is blown, the exchange prices your slow orders, not your average ones. Every line in the budget needs a percentile attached ("p99 strategy time ≤ 4 µs"), and periodic GC pauses, page faults and cache misses are exactly the events that live between p99 and max. Measure the distribution, budget the percentile you care about.

blocks.title: A 10-microsecond budget, allocated
items: Target: tick-to-trade ≤ $10\,\mu s$ on a kernel-stack path (illustrative).
Assign: kernel in/out $2 + 2 = 4\,\mu s$; decode $1$; decision $2$; risk gate $1$; encode $1$ - all µs.
Sum $= 4 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 9\,\mu s$; the remaining $1\,\mu s$ is **margin**, not spare budget, tails eat it.
Consequence: a decode costing $3\,\mu s$ is not 'a bit slow', it is $2\,\mu s$ stolen from the decision or the margin. Optimise where the budget says, not where the code is ugliest.

blocks.title: Latency buys survival, not wins
blocks.md: Being fast does not make your model right; being slow makes it wrong *later than the market*, your quote is stale exactly when someone knows something. The tail is what hurts: the slow 1% of your quotes is the 1% that gets picked off. That is why budgets carry margin and why percentiles (final lesson of this module) outrank averages.

Propagation is fixed. Light in fibre travels at ≈ $2 \times 10^8$ m/s, giving the handy anchor **≈ 5 µs per km one-way** (approximate). An 80 km link therefore costs ≈ $80 \times 5 = 400\,\mu s$ one-way, forty times the entire compute budget of the worked example above. This is why firms pay for colocation and microwave paths: distance is the one line item no compiler flag touches. Everything in the *processing* rows, by contrast, is negotiable, and that is where the rest of this module lives.

guidedExercise.prompt: Measured (approximate) stage costs on one path, in µs: kernel in 2.1, decode 0.4, decision 1.2, risk 0.3, encode+kernel out 1.5. (a) Total? (b) With an $8\,\mu s$ budget, how much margin remains? (c) Which stage is the obvious next optimisation target and why?
hints: Add the stages; margin = budget, total.
Target the stage with the largest cost you can actually influence.
guidedExercise.solution: (a) $2.1 + 0.4 + 1.2 + 0.3 + 1.5 = 5.5\,\mu s$. (b) $8 - 5.5 = 2.5\,\mu s$ of margin. (c) Kernel in/out at $3.6\,\mu s$ combined is the biggest *influenceable* cost (kernel-bypass techniques target it), then the decision at 1.2. Propagation is absent from this list precisely because software cannot change it.

independentExercise.prompt: Two firms connect Chicago and New York, ≈ 1,100 km of route (illustrative). (a) Estimate one-way fibre propagation using ≈ 5 µs/km. (b) A microwave path is near line-of-sight: even if perfectly straight, what is its physical floor using ≈ 3.3 µs/km (light in air)? (c) Roughly how much one-way time does microwave buy over fibre?
hints: Light in air is close to the vacuum speed of 3x10^8 m/s, hence ≈ 3.3 µs/km.
independentExercise.solution: (a) $1{,}100 \times 5 = 5{,}500\,\mu s = 5.5$ ms one-way (approximate). (b) $1{,}100 \times 3.3 = 3{,}630\,\mu s ≈ 3.6$ ms floor (approximate; real paths bend, so actual is higher). (c) Order of $5.5 - 3.6 ≈ 1.9$ ms saved one-way, the reason microwave links exist despite costing millions.

commonMistakes: Treating vendor 'typical latency' numbers as guarantees, they are orders of magnitude until measured on your path.
Spending the margin in the happy path; margin exists for tails.
Optimising arithmetic while ignoring the 1-2 µs kernel overhead in front of it (approximate).
Forgetting propagation in budgets that span distance.
realWorldApplication: Firms publish tick-to-trade figures measured on percentile distributions across the whole path; procurement decisions (colocation racks, NICs, switches) are argued in latency budgets like the one in this lesson.
quantFinanceApplication: Every microsecond of quote latency widens the window for adverse selection, so the budget directly bounds how tight a market maker can safely quote.
summary: Tick-to-trade = packet in -> decision -> order out; budgets name every stage and its µs allowance.
Orders of magnitude (approximate): kernel path 1-2 µs/direction, parse ~0.1 µs, switch hops ~0.1-0.5 µs, fibre ≈ 5 µs/km.
Propagation is fixed physics; processing is negotiable, optimise where the budget says.
Always keep margin: the tail (p99+) is what consumes unallocated time.

quiz.prompt: On a kernel-stack path, which component typically dominates tick-to-trade?
options: The OS network stack, syscalls and copies
The price-time priority matching at the venue
Serialisation of the order into JSON
quiz.explanation: Kernel overhead runs ~1-2 µs per direction (approximate) while the arithmetic of a decision is nanoseconds, which is why kernel bypass exists.

quiz.prompt: Using the ≈ 5 µs/km fibre rule of thumb, what is the one-way propagation of an 80 km link, in µs?
quiz.explanation: $80 \times 5 = 400\,\mu s$ (approximate anchor: light in glass ≈ $2 \times 10^8$ m/s).

quiz.prompt: Your total budget is 10 µs and the decode stage measures 3.5 µs. How much remains for every other stage combined?
quiz.explanation: $10 - 3.5 = 6.5\,\mu s$. A stage overshoot is a direct subtraction from everyone else, that is what a budget means.

options: Write down a per-stage budget and defend it
Measure each stage separately with profiling
Optimise the code with the most lines first
quiz.explanation: Budgets are written, measured and defended with margin; 'biggest file first' optimises effort, not latency.

quiz.prompt: Why can't software fix the ≈ 5 µs/km fibre cost?
options: Because fibre is cheaper than microwave
It is propagation physics: light in glass at ≈ 2x10^8 m/s
quiz.explanation: Propagation delay is distance divided by speed of light in the medium, fixed by physics. Only shorter or faster paths (colocation, microwave) change it.

quiz.prompt: Why is a single end-to-end stopwatch insufficient for optimising tick-to-trade?
quiz.modelAnswer: A total tells you that you are slow, not where. Each stage has a different owner and a different fix (kernel bypass, parsing, decision design), so costs must be attributed per stage with profiling before optimising anything.
quiz.explanation: Optimisation needs attribution: without per-stage measurements you may spend weeks polishing a stage that costs 1% of the path.

flashcards.back: ≈ 5 µs per km one-way (light in glass ≈ 2x10^8 m/s). Clearly approximate.
Time from a market-data packet arriving at the NIC to the order packet leaving it, decision included.
Budget minus allocated stage costs; reserved for tail events, not for new features.
Propagation physics (distance / medium speed). Everything on the processing path is negotiable.
